opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the underappreciated asymmetries in how people imagine things going. The default picture of an intelligence explosion is that it happens inside a small number of frontier AI companies, because they're the ones who have the best models first, they have the compute, and they have the most direct incentive to point those models at AI R&D. So if you're an external group, whether that's a safety research nonprofit, a government agency, or an academic lab, you're starting from a position where the most capable AI labor in the world is, at least initially, sitting behind someone else's API or not available at all.

There are a few layers to the challenge. The first is just access. During the most important window, the very best models may not be publicly deployed. Companies might keep their strongest systems internal for competitive reasons, for security reasons, or because they haven't finished safety testing. So the external group might be working with a model that's six months or a year behind, and in an intelligence explosion, six months could be an enormous gap in capability.

The second layer is compute. Even if you have access to a strong model, running it at the scale where it matters, thousands or millions of copies working in parallel, takes a huge amount of inference compute. That's where the labs and hyperscalers have a structural advantage. An external group might be able to run a handful of instances while the lab is running something like a whole research organization's worth of AI workers. If you think the key outputs, like alignment research, evaluations, and security work, scale with the amount of AI labor you can throw at them, then compute becomes the binding constraint.

The third layer is the scaffolding and know-how. Getting real research productivity out of AI agents isn't just plugging in a model. You need infrastructure for long-horizon tasks, for verification, for coordinating many agents, and for checking their work. The labs will be developing that tooling for their own internal use, and it may not be shared, or it may be tightly coupled to their own systems.

So what do you do about it? I think it pushes in a few directions. One is that it makes the case for pre-commitments and agreements now, while things are calmer, where labs agree to set aside some fraction of their compute or give structured access to vetted external researchers, especially for safety and oversight work. Another is that governments probably need to think about whether they should be building or securing their own compute capacity, so that independent evaluation and safety work isn't wholly dependent on the goodwill of the companies being overseen. And a third is that external groups should be getting good at using AI labor right now, building the workflows and institutional muscle, so that when more capable systems arrive they can actually absorb them productively rather than spending months figuring out how.

The deeper worry is about checks and balances. If essentially all of the world's highest-quality cognitive labor is concentrated in a couple of organizations, then the usual ways society keeps powerful actors accountable, like independent researchers, journalists, regulators, and civil society, could be outpaced. Making sure some meaningful share of AI labor ends up in the hands of people whose job is to scrutinize and course-correct seems really important, and it's much easier to arrange that before the explosion than in the middle of it.

r001.rationale: It says external groups may have to use models six months or a year behind frontier companies’ strongest internal systems, creating a potentially enormous capability gap.

r002.rationale: It discusses the compute required to run AI labor, but does not explain that providers may prefer to use that compute to train more powerful systems instead of selling AI labor.

r003.rationale: It suggests building or securing compute capacity, but does not propose investments that gain value as compute prices rise as a hedge against the future cost of obtaining AI labor.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the things I worry about most when I imagine how an intelligence explosion actually plays out, as opposed to how it plays out in the abstract.

The basic picture is that at some point, the frontier labs have systems that are essentially automating their own AI research. And once that's happening, the amount of cognitive labor available inside the lab explodes. You have the equivalent of millions of very capable researchers running around the clock, and the lab is using most of that to go faster: to improve the next model, to scale up, to stay ahead of competitors.

Now imagine you're an external group. Maybe you're a safety-focused nonprofit, maybe you're a government agency, maybe you're an academic lab, maybe you're a third-party auditor. Your job depends on having access to roughly comparable AI labor, because otherwise you just cannot keep up. You can't evaluate a system that's thinking a thousand times faster than you using human researchers alone. You can't audit the training process, you can't check alignment claims, you can't do independent interpretability work at the scale that would be needed.

And the problem is that the labor you need is exactly the labor that's most valuable to the people who have it. The lab has every incentive to pour its best models into its own research loop, because that's what wins the race. Selling or lending that capacity to outsiders is a direct hit to their own progress. So even in a world where the lab is well-intentioned, there's a structural pull toward hoarding.

Then you layer on the practical obstacles. The most capable models are probably not released externally at all during this period. The ones that are released are often behind, or rate-limited, or heavily wrapped in restrictions. And the compute to run them at scale is itself scarce and expensive. So an external group ends up with something like last year's model, at a fraction of the throughput, trying to oversee this year's model. That gap compounds very quickly once things are moving fast.

There's also a subtler problem, which is that even if you do get access, you're renting labor from the very entity you're supposed to be checking. If the lab controls the model you're using to evaluate the lab, there are all kinds of ways that can go wrong, from benign ones, like the model just having the lab's assumptions baked in, to much more concerning ones if the model itself is misaligned and has a stake in how the evaluation turns out.

So when I think about what we should be doing now, a lot of it comes down to establishing the norms and infrastructure before the crunch. Things like: committed compute allocations for external evaluators that are set in advance and can't be quietly renegotiated when things get competitive. Access agreements that give third parties real model access, not a degraded version. Some form of government capacity so that there's at least one well-resourced actor whose job is oversight and who isn't in the race. And honestly, just getting people used to the idea that a slice of the AI labor pie has to go to checking the work, the same way we accept that a company has to have auditors even though auditors slow things down.

Because I think the failure mode is not that anyone decides outsiders shouldn't have access. It's that in the moment, every marginal unit of AI labor looks more valuable going into the next model than into oversight, and nobody makes the deliberate choice to carve some out. If we haven't built that in ahead of time, I don't expect it to appear on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says external groups may be stuck with “last year's model” at a fraction of the throughput while overseeing “this year's model,” and that the gap compounds as progress accelerates.

r002.rationale: It explains that providers have an incentive to keep AI labor for their own research because lending or selling it could slow their progress. It does not say that selling the labor may be prohibitively expensive because the provider could instead use the compute to train more powerful systems.

r003.rationale: The response proposes advance compute allocations and access agreements, but it does not propose investments that gain value as compute prices rise as a hedge against future AI labor costs.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether access to AI labor remains something you can buy on a market, or whether it becomes a resource that a small number of actors are allocating strategically.

An external group might think, “We’ll raise money, and then when the models are good enough, we’ll hire a bunch of AI researchers to work on alignment.” But the same models that can do alignment research can also help build the next generation of AI. So you’re competing with a use of that labor that could be extraordinarily valuable to the companies developing it. Having enough money at today’s prices doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll have access when you need it.

There’s also a timing problem. If progress is moving very quickly, you can’t necessarily wait until the capabilities are obvious and then start negotiating access, setting up your infrastructure, and figuring out how to manage the research. By the time you’ve done that, the frontier could have moved substantially.

So I’d want an external group to think about securing access in advance, and about what that access actually includes. Is it access to the best models? Enough compute to run them at scale? The ability to use them for the research you want to do? Those are different things. And I wouldn’t treat a promise of future access as automatically resolving the problem, because the incentives to honor that promise could change a lot during an intelligence explosion.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes access to the best models from other kinds of access, but does not say that companies’ best internal systems could outpace the best systems available to external groups.

r002.rationale: It says companies may value AI labor for building the next generation of AI, but does not explain that a provider could use the compute to train more powerful systems, making labor prohibitively expensive to sell.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose investments that gain value as compute prices rise as a hedge against future AI labor costs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central challenge is that access to AI labor today doesn’t necessarily translate into access during an intelligence explosion. You might have a relationship with an AI company, or funding to buy a lot of API access, but the amount of intelligence you can actually get could change very quickly relative to what the leading companies have internally.

If those companies are using their best systems to do AI research, and those systems are producing the next generation of systems, then being even a little bit behind could become a very big deal. You could have lots of AI labor in an absolute sense and still not have enough to keep up with the questions you’re trying to answer.

So I’d want to ask: What is the actual arrangement that gives this external group access? Does it include the most capable models? Does it include enough compute to run them at the scale they need? And will that arrangement hold up when access becomes much more valuable, and the company has strong reasons to use that compute itself?

That makes me somewhat skeptical of plans that are just, ‘We’ll raise money and hire AI workers when the time comes.’ I think you’d want to do a lot of the institutional work in advance, while recognizing that even a fairly strong commitment might be hard to make robust to such a rapidly changing situation.

r001.rationale: It says external access may fall behind what leading companies have internally, and that the gap could grow quickly as their best systems produce the next generation.

r002.rationale: It notes that a company may prefer to use compute itself when access becomes valuable, but does not explain that selling AI labor could become prohibitively expensive because the provider could use the compute to train more capable systems.

r003.rationale: It recommends advance institutional work, but does not propose investments that gain value as compute prices rise as a hedge against future AI labor costs.
